title: Other states and districts can use kindergarten entry assessments to track students' progress toward reading proficiency
description: The article generalizes its Philadelphia indicator approach to other education agencies, recommending kindergarten entry assessments as a basis for progress monitoring toward grade 3 reading proficiency. It states that "Other states and districts could consider using kindergarten entry assessments to track students' progress towards reading proficiency." The principle rests on the demonstrated link between KEI scores and later grade 3 ELA outcomes in one district.

article_title: Understanding How International Students in the U.S. Are Using Conversational AI to Support Cross-Cultural Adaptation
citation: Nourian, L.; Callis, A.; Patterson, S.; Miao, J.; Heard, J.; Tigwell, G. W. (2026). Understanding How International Students in the U.S. Are Using Conversational AI to Support Cross-Cultural Adaptation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15127
title: Kim's stress-adaptation-growth framework of cross-cultural adaptation
description: The article frames its survey instrument using Kim's Cross-Cultural Adaptation framework, in which adaptation is "a dynamic process of 'stress-adaptation-growth'" where the challenges of cultural shock act as a catalyst for personal transformation. Stress is treated as a prerequisite for adapting and growing, forcing individuals to constantly learn new skills to operate in unfamiliar environments, making adaptation an iterative process of resolving tensions between cultural perspectives. The survey's parts map onto the framework's phases: challenges (stress), AI usage actions (adaptation), and growth.
requirements: The framework presupposes exposure to stressors in the host environment as the driver of adaptation and growth
constraints: The article applies it to first-time international students in the US who had not studied in another country before
target_learning_goals: learning new skills to operate in unfamiliar environments
examples: The survey's four parts were designed around the framework's phases: stress and challenges, adaptation actions with AI, and growth and improvement ratings

article_title: Retrieval-Augmented Tutoring for Algorithm Tracing and Problem-Solving in AI Education
citation: Mragisha Jain, Tirth Bhatt, Griffin Pitts, Aum Pandya, Peter Brusilovsky, Narges Norouzi, Arto Hellas, Juho Leinonen, Bita Akram. (2026). Retrieval-Augmented Tutoring for Algorithm Tracing and Problem-Solving in AI Education. Proceedings of the 21st Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2026), co-located with ACL 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12988
title: KITE: an intent-aware RAG tutoring architecture combining multi-stage retrieval with pedagogical response strategies
description: KITE (Knowledge-Informed Tutoring Engine) is a RAG-based intelligent tutoring system for course-grounded dialogue on algorithmic reasoning and problem-solving. As the article states, "the system includes five components: document preprocessing, embedding generation, multi-stage retrieval, intent-aware response generation, and session management." Each query is classified by pedagogical intent, and the classified intent determines the response strategy: grounded explanations for direct and conceptual questions, Socratic assessment for validation, diagnostic hint progressions for debugging, and step-by-step state-tracing for algorithm tracing. Retrieval combines dense bi-encoder search, hybrid scoring (70% dense, 30% BM25), MMR with λ = 0.7, cross-encoder reranking, and source-based boosting, passing the top eight chunks to GPT-5.
requirements: Requires course materials for document ingestion and a keyword and pattern-matching intent classifier to route queries to response strategies
constraints: The article notes strong retrieval alone does not ensure effective tutoring; responses may still be too direct or mismatched to the student's need
target_learners: university students in an Introduction to AI course
examples: For algorithm tracing queries, KITE retrieves procedural steps from course materials and applies them step by step, maintaining state variables such as OPEN lists and CLOSED sets

article_title: Examining the Effectiveness of School-Bullying Intervention Programs Globally: a Meta-analysis
citation: Hannah Gaffney, David P. Farrington, & Maria M. Ttofi. (2019). Examining the Effectiveness of School-Bullying Intervention Programs Globally: a Meta-analysis. International Journal of Bullying Prevention. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42380-019-0007-4
title: Four repeatedly evaluated anti-bullying programs: KiVa, OBPP, NoTrap!, and ViSC
description: Of 65 different school-based bullying programs in the meta-analysis, only four were evaluated more than twice across locations: KiVa, OBPP, NoTrap!, and ViSC. KiVa targets bystanders to reduce social rewards for bullies and includes a virtual-learning element; OBPP is a whole-school program operating at school, classroom, individual, and community levels; NoTrap! is a web-based program engaging students as peer-educators moderating an anti-bullying forum; ViSC is a 1-year train-the-trainer program with 13 student lessons. Table 1 compares their components.
requirements: Programs in the meta-analysis required an operational definition of school bullying, quantitative perpetration/victimization measures, and an experimental or quasi-experimental design with a control group
constraints: The article notes the four programs "incorporated quite similar intervention components," with NoTrap! the most different, yet their effectiveness varied greatly
target_learners: School children and adolescents, primarily primary and secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Reducing school-bullying perpetration and victimization, and building empathy, self-efficacy, and anti-bullying attitudes
examples: KiVa includes classroom lesson plans with group discussion, role-play, anti-bullying videos, and an anti-bullying computer game; ViSC students complete 13 lessons and a class project.

title: Kindergarten pre-reading screening battery (CTOPP, RAN/RAS, YARC LSK, KBIT-2, WRMT Word ID)
description: A 30–45 minute individually administered assessment battery used to derive the latent profiles. It includes CTOPP Elision and Blending Words for the PA composite, CTOPP Nonword Repetition for verbal short-term memory, RAN/RAS Colors and Objects subtests where "the raw score is the time to name all items", YARC Letter Sound Knowledge, KBIT-2 Matrices for non-verbal IQ, and WRMT Word ID to classify readers versus non-readers. title: Assess kindergarten language and number naming to inform targeted instruction and interventions for children at risk of arithmetic difficulties
description: The article argues that knowledge of kindergarten predictors should guide early support: "Such knowledge is necessary in order to inform targeted instruction and interventions that address the needs of children at risk". article_title: Transfer between reading comprehension and word-problem solving among children with learning difficulty in both domains.
citation: Fuchs, L. S., Seethaler, P. M., Sterba, S. K., Fuchs, D., Cutting, L. E., Mancilla-Martinez, J., Martin, B. L. N., & Espinas, D. (2024). Transfer between Reading Comprehension and Word-Problem Solving among Children with Learning Difficulty in Both Domains. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000911
title: Kintsch and Greeno's model of word-problem solving as text processing
description: The study's theoretical framework is Kintsch and Greeno's (1985) model of WPS, rooted in discourse-processing theory. It holds that WP representations, like other text, have three components: a coherent text structure, a situation model supplemented with world knowledge about quantity relations, and knowledge of problem models that formalizes relations and guides solution strategies within schema. The article states "The model assumes that word-problem (WP) representations, as with other forms of text, have three components." Building these representations makes strong demands on memory, attentive behavior, reasoning, and language comprehension.
requirements: Problem solvers must coordinate world knowledge about quantity relations with problem-model knowledge to build representations
constraints: Incorrect solutions may arise from text-processing failures or from computational error, so the model does not attribute all WPS errors to text processing
target_learners: elementary students solving arithmetic word problems
target_learning_goals: constructing mental representations of word problems
examples: The article walks through a combine-schema puppy/kitten problem showing how propositions are stored in working memory and the schema is filled (Part 1 + Part 2 = Total)

article_title: Measurements of the physical growth of two children.
citation: King, Irving. (1930). Measurements of the Physical Growth of Two Children. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: A Virtual Space for Children to Meet and Practice Chinese
citation: Mei Si. (2015). A Virtual Space for Children to Meet and Practice Chinese. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:271–290. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0035-7
title: Four Kinect-enabled multiplayer virtual Chinese practice environments
description: A Unity-based multi-user system with a central server and Kinect-equipped clients, plus a mouse-and-keyboard fallback, in which users control virtual characters with body movements and talk via integrated voice chat. Four environments were built: Cao Chung Weighing an Elephant, The Elephant and the Blind Men, a school café, and a chat room, each embedding narratives and puzzles. The environments were "designed as supplementary materials to the learners' regular Chinese classes" and support different levels of open-ended conversation with an emphasis on social interaction.

Integrated voice chat so users need no special operations to talk with each other

Configuration of Environment 2's object set is not fully automated; the game must be rebuilt after adding new materials

target_learning_goals: Mandarin Chinese vocabulary, sentences, directions and movements
examples: In the evaluation, Environment 1 was used for three classes and Environment 2 for three classes; teachers led the class in reciting action and object names while two students played

citation: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung, C.W. Dawson. (2007). The Effect of a Computer-Based Cartooning Tool On Children's Cartoons and Written Stories. Loughborough University Institutional Repository. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/
title: The kineikonic mode: filming and editing as the two defining characteristics of moving image texts
description: The article adopts Burn and Parker's account of the moving image as a mode defined by two characteristics: filming (framing and composing a scene into actual or notional camera shots) and editing (ordering shots so juxtapositions create meaning). It quotes the definition that the mode "operates as a combinatorial mode which assembles and integrates other modes (speech, image, gesture, music) through its own 'grammar' of filming and editing", and notes it extends to comic strips, storyboards and games, which grounds the design of the study's cartooning tools.
requirements: Interpreting an artefact as a moving image text requires identifiable shot framing and some form of shot sequencing or ordering
constraints: The article warns, citing Burn and Leach, of over-using language analogies since the moving image is not precisely a language
target_learners: primary school children in Years 5 and 6 (ages 9 to 11)
target_learning_goals: moving image literacy alongside print literacy
storytelling and narrative concepts such as characterisation, setting and pace
examples: The study operationalises filming as a camera point-of-view control with shot distances and editing as an explicit left-to-right sequence bar for ordering shots

article_title: Evaluating the impact of simulation on patient outcomes in pediatric and neonatal critical care: a systematic review and critical appraisal of the evidence.
citation: Zanin A, Poletto E, Mencia S, Gawronski O, Jourdain G. (2026). Evaluating the impact of simulation on patient outcomes in pediatric and neonatal critical care: a systematic review and critical appraisal of the evidence. European Journal of Pediatrics 185(5):302. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-026-06925-3
title: Kirkpatrick four-level model with the Level 4a/4b distinction as a framework for evaluating simulation-based education
description: The review organizes its evidence synthesis around the Kirkpatrick model, "a widely used four-level framework for evaluating the effectiveness of educational interventions, including SBE". Level 1 assesses reaction, Level 2 learning, Level 3 behavior in clinical practice, and Level 4 results; the review adopts the subdivision of Level 4 into 4a (system-level process metrics such as response times and protocol adherence) and 4b (direct patient outcomes such as mortality and complications). This distinction structures its primary outcome coding and thematic synthesis.
requirements: Outcomes must be coded as 4a or 4b according to whether the primary metric is a process-based system measure or a direct patient health indicator
constraints: The review notes a fundamental challenge lies in capturing the complex transfer of learning from simulation environments to real-world clinical practice
target_learners: healthcare providers and trainees in pediatric and neonatal intensive care
target_learning_goals: clinical skills and teamwork in resuscitation and critical care procedures
examples: The review mapped each included study's outcomes to levels L1, L2, L3, 4a, and 4b in a structured table

article_title: Technology-enhanced training in basic robotic surgical skills: a systematic review.
citation: Shakir T, Lingam G, Boal M, Francis N, Chand M. (2026). Technology-enhanced training in basic robotic surgical skills: a systematic review. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-026-03633-w
title: Kirkpatrick model mapping as the organising framework for evaluating technology-enhanced surgical training evidence
description: The review uses the Kirkpatrick model of training evaluation as its organising axis, mapping each included study's reported outcomes to a level: level 1 reaction, level 2 learning (simulator scores, kinematic metrics, R-OSATS), level 3 transfer to operative behaviour, and level 4 patient outcomes. It reports that "the available evidence is concentrated at level 2 (learning — simulator scores, kinematic metrics, R-OSATS)". This framework lets the review show that no study reached transfer or patient-level outcomes, bounding what the technology evidence can support.
requirements: Studies must report outcomes classifiable into Kirkpatrick levels for the mapping to characterise educational impact
constraints: No included study reported level 3 or level 4 outcomes, limiting extrapolation to clinical performance
examples: The review assigned each of the 17 included studies a Kirkpatrick level in Table 1, finding sixteen at level 2 and one at level 1

article_title: Innovative technologies in psychiatry education: a systematic review.
citation: Mokhtari Saba, Mokhtari Asieh, Shariat Seyed Vahid, Nazeri Astaneh Ali, Shalbafan Mohammadreza. (2026). Innovative technologies in psychiatry education: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09573-1
title: Kirkpatrick and Miller framework mapping of psychiatry education technology evidence
description: The review maps its included studies onto two established evaluation frameworks to locate the evidence's level. According to Kirkpatrick's model, most studies demonstrated effects at Level 2 (learning), with only a few reporting Level 1 (learner satisfaction) and none reaching Levels 3 or 4. On Miller's pyramid, most interventions addressed the 'knows' and 'knows how' levels, while HFSs and immersive VR achieved the 'shows how' level. The review uses this mapping to highlight "the critical gap in evidence for their long-term impact on professional practice and patient care."
requirements: Studies must report outcomes classifiable into Kirkpatrick levels or Miller pyramid levels for the mapping to apply
constraints: None of the included studies evaluated the 'does' level of actual clinical performance or patient outcomes (Kirkpatrick Levels 3–4)
target_learning_goals: attitudes such as empathy and stigma reduction
examples: The review classified the nine included trials' outcomes (knowledge tests, diagnostic reasoning tasks, OSATS skill demonstrations) within the two frameworks' levels

citation: Blackburn, J. J., Robinson, J. S., & Kacal, A. (2015). Determining the effects of reflection type and cognitive style on students' content knowledge. Journal of Agricultural Education, 56(3), 195-209. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2015.03195
title: Kirton's Adaption-Innovation Theory (KAIT) as a framework for cognitive style in learning
description: Kirton's Adaption-Innovation Theory holds that all individuals are creative and all solve problems, but how people prefer to solve problems can differ. Cognitive style is defined as the preferred way in which people respond to and seek to bring about change, and is a stable characteristic that does not deviate due to time or experiences. The theory frames cognitive style as a continuum ranging from more adaptive (preferring structured problems and better solutions) to more innovative (preferring loosely structured problems and different solutions). The study used this theory as its framework and measured cognitive style with the 32-item KAI inventory.
requirements: Cognitive style is assessed via Kirton's Adaption-Innovation Inventory (KAI), a 32-item instrument with scores ranging from 32 to 160 and a theoretical mean of 96
constraints: The KAI was designed to be utilized with working adults, though it has been used in additional contexts including with teenagers and educational settings
target_learning_goals: understanding individual differences in problem-solving preference as they relate to learning
examples: Students scoring 95 or below were classified as more adaptive and those scoring 96 or higher as more innovative; post-hoc reliability in this sample yielded a Cronbach's alpha of .79

examples: In the study's scoring procedure, selecting a killer option on any of the 19 cases resulted in no credit for that item regardless of other selections.
